title: What's this? — three noun genders
goal: Name the things around you, read a noun's gender from its last letter, and attach adjectives that change to match their noun — across three genders and three numbers at once.
bekal: guess a noun's gender from its last letter, and spot the handful of feminine words in disguise
make adjectives agree: *nov slovar*, *nova knjiga*, *novo okno*
use *to je* to introduce things, and *ta / tisti* to point at them

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Nova soba
dialogs.intro: Maja comes to see Budi's rented room for the first time. Some of the things in it belonged to the previous tenant.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: To je slovar. Nov je in zelo debel.
lines.id: It's a dictionary. It's new and really thick.
lines.literal: this is dictionary. new is and very thick.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: In tam? Kaj sta tisti dve knjigi?
lines.id: And over there? What are those two books?
lines.literal: and there? what are-two those-two-f two books?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Two old textbooks. They're not mine.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Od Luke. Miza je tudi njegova.
lines.literal: from Luka. table is also his-f.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Aha. In to okno je veliko — soba je svetla.
lines.id: I see. And this window is big — the room is bright.
lines.literal: aha. and this window is big — room is bright.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Over there. It's small, but comfortable.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: Great. The room is really nice.

notes: **To je never changes.** To introduce anything at all, the form is always *To je…* — *To je slovar* (masculine), *To je knjiga* (feminine), *To je okno* (neuter). Only the number changes: *To sta…* for two, *To so…* for three or more. So the most useful sentence in this unit is the one that asks nothing of you.

**Adjectives stick to their noun's gender.** *Nov slovar*, *nova knjiga*, *novo okno* — one adjective, three endings. English writes "new" the same way every time; Slovenian doesn't have that option. The good news: the endings match the noun's endings exactly, so once you know the gender, the adjective follows by itself.

**Nista moja — both are dual.** *Nista* is the negative of *sta*, and *moja* here is not the feminine form but the masculine dual of *moj*. Twin forms like this will pop up often; the verb is always what gives them away.

**Čigav = "whose", and it's an adjective itself.** So it changes too: *Čigav slovar?* (masculine), *Čigava knjiga?* (feminine), *Čigavo okno?* (neuter), *Čigava sta?* (two). English gets by with "whose" for all of them.

**Hrupno and svetla — adjectives describing a state.** In *Soba je svetla*, the adjective is feminine because *soba* is feminine. But in *Zunaj je hrupno* there's no noun at all — so Slovenian uses the **neuter** as its fallback form. The same pattern is used for weather in unit 16: *Toplo je* (it's warm), *Mrzlo je* (it's cold).

grammars.title: Three noun genders — read from the last letter
body: Unlike German or French, Slovenian noun gender can almost always be **seen**, not memorized. The last letter tells you.
after: Those three lines cover maybe nine out of ten nouns you'll meet at A1. Notice that *avto* (car) ends in *-o* but is still **masculine** — it's a loanword that brought its own gender, like *radio* and *kino*.

There's one group of exceptions you really do need to memorize: **feminine words ending in a consonant**. There aren't many, but they're all common: *noč* (night), *stvar* (thing), *misel* (thought), *ljubezen* (love), *pomoč* (help), *jesen* (autumn).

grammars.title: Adjectives: three genders times three numbers
body: This is a table to look at once in full, then you can leave it. It shows the adjective *lep* (beautiful) attached to nouns of all three genders.
after: What helps: **the adjective ending and the noun ending rhyme**. *Nova miza*, *novi mizi*, *nove mize* — once your ear is used to it, your hand picks the ending without opening the table.

Watch for one neat twin: the form **lepa** appears twice — for one feminine thing (*lepa knjiga*) and for two masculine things (*lepa slovarja*). Again, the verb gives it away: *je* for one, *sta* for two.

grammars.title: Ta in tisti — this and that
body: Slovenian splits distance in two, just like English. Both words are adjectives, so both change.
after: Don't mix up **ta** as a pointer (*ta knjiga* = this book) with **to** as a sentence opener (*To je knjiga* = this is a book). The first attaches to a noun; the second stands alone and never changes.
In everyday speech, Slovenians often add *-le*: *tale* (this one here), *tistile* (that one there). It adds a finger-pointing feel, and you'll hear it constantly at the market.

blocks.text: The fastest way to lock in the three genders is to learn each noun together with an adjective, not on its own. So don't learn *miza*; learn *velika miza*.

Look at **računalnik** (computer): the *l* in the middle falls before a consonant, so it's said **rah-choo-NOW-neek**. This word is also a good example of the Slovenian habit of resisting loanwords — many languages use "computer"; Slovenian built its own word from *računati* (to calculate).

blocks.title: Three sentences that unlock every object
items: *Kaj je to?* — What's this? The answer: *To je …*
*Kako se reče "table" po slovensko?* — How do you say "table" in Slovenian?

blocks.text: These pairs cover almost everything you'll need to say about things at A1. All are given in the masculine singular — the dictionary form.

Look at *grd* — an adjective with no vowel at all, said **guhrt** with a schwa before the *r*, just as promised on the pronunciation page. And *poceni* (cheap) is the only one on this list that **never changes form**: *poceni knjiga*, *poceni slovar*, *poceni okno*. It's the one free gift on this page.
To strengthen, put *zelo* (very) in front: *zelo velik*, *zelo lepa*, *zelo poceni*. To soften, use *precej* (fairly) or *malo* (a bit): *precej velik*, *malo star*.

This room is small, but comfortable.
